v.why: Extra layers compound the instability of very large Adam steps, causing divergence or dead ReLUs, so adding depth hurts more when the learning rate is high.
Strong L2 shrinks every weight matrix, and the shrinkage compounds across layers so signal and gradients vanish more in deeper nets.
The L2 penalty sums over many more weights in a wider net, so strong alpha over-shrinks it into underfitting.
A single hidden layer makes width the main source of representational capacity, so widening helps more than in deeper nets.
Narrow layers limit capacity and extra layers relieve this through composition, while wide nets already have enough capacity.
Adam's per-parameter steps sum over thousands of units, so wide nets overshoot sooner as the learning rate rises.
Large batches give few updates in a fixed epoch budget and low-noise gradients, so a bigger step compensates and is tolerated.
The L2 term is scaled by one over batch size in common MLP implementations, so a larger batch weakens an otherwise crushing penalty.
With small batches the per-batch L2 penalty is relatively larger, so raising alpha over-shrinks the weights and underfits.
At a low learning rate the net is update-starved, so smaller batches supply many more steps.
